name: Cholecystokinin (CCK-8)

b.x: A single IV infusion of CCK-8 cuts how much healthy men eat, and the effect grows with the dose. That finding, from Brennan and colleagues in a controlled study of 10 healthy men [1], captured what the gut already knew: cholecystokinin is the body's fastest brake on eating. CCK-8 (also called CCK-8S for its sulfated form; CAS 25126-32-3) is the most bioactive circulating fragment of the 33-amino-acid hormone cholecystokinin, first isolated from porcine intestinal mucosa in the 1960s. Duodenal and jejunal I-cells release it within minutes of detecting dietary fat and protein. It locks onto CCK1 receptors on vagal nerve endings and sends satiety signals straight to the brainstem. Simultaneously, it contracts the gallbladder, pumps pancreatic enzymes, and slows gastric emptying. Think of it as a coordinated digestive and satiety broadcast that peaks in under 15 minutes and vanishes in under five. The synthetic version, sincalide (Kinevac), received FDA approval in 1976 for gallbladder ejection fraction testing. Radiologists still use it daily. Native CCK-8 has no therapeutic approval; its half-life of about 1.3 minutes ([PMID 4014106](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/4014106/)) and IV-only validated route make chronic dosing impractical. Rehfeld's 2025 review [2] confirmed that current obesity research has shifted toward protease-resistant CCK1-selective analogs rather than native CCK-8. Community use is nonexistent: zero Reddit threads, zero biohacker protocols, zero self-administration reports exist anywhere online.

CCK-8 binds two G-protein-coupled receptor subtypes. CCK1 receptors sit mostly in the periphery: gallbladder smooth muscle, pancreatic acinar cells, and vagal afferent nerve terminals lining the stomach and duodenum. CCK2 receptors concentrate in the central nervous system. When CCK-8 docks with either receptor, it kicks off a Gq/11 signaling cascade. Phospholipase C generates IP3 and DAG. IP3 releases calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum; DAG activates protein kinase C. In pancreatic acinar cells, that calcium surge triggers exocytosis of zymogen granules packed with digestive enzymes. In gallbladder smooth muscle, the same cascade produces contraction and bile ejection. The satiety pathway runs through CCK1 receptors on vagal afferent nerve endings. Receptor activation fires action potentials up the vagus nerve to the nucleus tractus solitarius in the brainstem. From there, signals relay to hypothalamic feeding centers to suppress appetite and terminate meals. CCK-8 also slows gastric emptying through both vagal reflexes and direct smooth muscle action, keeping nutrients in contact with absorptive epithelium longer. In the brain, CCK-8 modulates dopaminergic, serotonergic, and GABAergic neurotransmission. The closely related fragment CCK-4 is a validated panicogenic agent in human studies; CCK-8 has weaker anxiogenic properties through CCK2 receptors. Some tissues also see adenylyl cyclase activation via Gs coupling, raising cAMP and activating protein kinase A.
Cholecystokinin (CCK-8) benefits center on satiety signaling and digestive coordination in controlled research settings.
Energy intake at a buffet meal fell as the IV dose rose in 10 healthy men (Brennan et al. 2008) [1].
Gallbladder ejection fraction drops 40 to 70 percent within 5 to 15 minutes of IV administration, the basis for its FDA-approved diagnostic use since 1976.
Pancreatic enzyme secretion peaks rapidly after CCK1 receptor activation in acinar cells, improving nutrient digestion during research protocols.
Gastric emptying delay extends nutrient contact with absorptive epithelium; this mechanism works with leptin and other anorexigenic signals for stronger satiety.
Research interest in anxiolytic and pain modulation pathways through CCK2 receptors in the CNS, though human therapeutic applications remain unproven.
Science Only
Scientific Evidence
Based on 10 key studies · FDA-approved
CCK-8 is a validated endogenous satiety hormone with strong IV human evidence for meal termination, gallbladder contraction, and gastric emptying delay.
Dosing studied: 0.02–0.04 mcg/kg IV bolus (1.4–2.8 mcg for 70 kg adult); max infusion protocol 0.12 mcg/kg over 50 min (~8.4 mcg for 70 kg). No validated human SC dosing exists.

Its half-life of about 1.3 min makes it impractical as a therapeutic agent. All validated human administration is IV only. The FDA-approved synthetic equivalent (sincalide/Kinevac) is approved solely for diagnostic gallbladder imaging since 1976.
Key Study

Brennan IM et al. Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab 2008;295(6):E1487-94; PMID 18957613: dose-dependent effects of CCK-8 on antropyloroduodenal motility, GI hormones, appetite, and energy intake in healthy men (gold-standard human pharmacodynamic study)
Limitations

All validated human data is IV only. No SC bioavailability data in humans. No approved obesity or therapeutic indication for native CCK-8. Extremely short half-life precludes sustained effect. Tachyphylaxis with repeated use via CCK1 receptor desensitization. 2025 research interest has shifted toward long-acting CCK1-selective analogs (not native CCK-8).

Science-Only Evidence

No community use exists for CCK-8. Scientific evidence for its endogenous role is strong; evidence for exogenous therapeutic application is limited to research settings with IV administration. The compound has no biohacker or self-optimization profile.
Speculative Research use only; no established injectable human dosing protocol

CCK-8 is not a typical research peptide. All validated human dosing is intravenous, and most people encounter it only as sincalide (Kinevac) during a gallbladder imaging study. Gray-market research vials are unsuitable for anything going IV. You need the sulfated form (CCK-8S). The sulfated tyrosine at position 7 is required for full CCK1 receptor potency; the non-sulfated version has roughly 1000-fold lower affinity. If satiety and gallbladder effects don't materialize, wrong form is the first thing to check. The Certificate of Analysis names which form a vial contains. The only sourced setup comes from the Kinevac label. A 5 mcg vial plus 5 mL of Sterile Water for Injection makes 1 mcg/mL (section 2.2). A 70 kg adult's 0.02 to 0.04 mcg/kg dose is then 1.4 to 2.8 mL. No published source gives a stock setup for a 1 mg research vial, which holds 200 times as much peptide. Kinevac vials are single use. Keep the mixed vial at room temperature and discard it after 8 hours; a diluted infusion goes after 1 hour (section 2.2). Store lyophilized research powder at -20C desiccated.
Cycling
Not cycled. The Kinevac label gives one IV dose per imaging study, plus a second if the gallbladder has not contracted in 15 minutes (section 2.1). No on/off cycle has been published.
Cholecystokinin (CCK-8)

CCK1 receptor desensitization occurs with continuous or repeated high-frequency CCK-8 exposure via β-arrestin-mediated receptor internalization. Vagal afferent CCK1 receptors on gastric and duodenal mucosal terminals show reduced sensitivity with sustained stimulation. In research settings, intermittent per-meal administration is standard, not continuous daily cycling. This page sets no cycle: no published human study has tested an on/off cycle.

Reduced gallbladder contraction amplitude on successive IV stimulations
Tachyphylaxis to GI motility effects within a research session
Reduced meal-size suppression efficacy over successive study visits
Dosing tiers, timing, and cycle length
Verify the peptide is CCK-8 sulfated (CCK-8S) with HPLC purity of 98 percent or higher and confirmed molecular weight of 1143.25 Da on the CoA.

Reconstitute The sourced setup is the Kinevac label's: add 5 mL of Sterile Water for Injection to the 5 mcg vial for 1 mcg/mL (section 2.2). No published source gives a stock setup for a 1 mg research vial.

Calculate your dose The label dose is 0.02 mcg/kg, then 0.04 mcg/kg if the gallbladder has not contracted within 15 minutes (section 2.1). For a 70 kg adult, that is 1.4 to 2.8 mcg, or 1.4 to 2.8 mL at 1 mcg/mL.

Give it as the label does The standard is an IV injection over 30 to 60 seconds. Nausea and cramping can occur with that route (section 5.3). To reduce them, the label offers an infusion of 0.12 mcg/kg in 100 mL of 0.9 percent saline over 50 minutes (section 2.1).
Begin 15 to 30 minutes before meal initiation if studying satiety effects.

Monitor heart rate and blood pressure continuously throughout the infusion and for 15 minutes after completion. Have epinephrine available for anaphylaxis risk from preservatives. Stop immediately for severe abdominal pain, HR below 50 bpm, or systolic BP below 90 mmHg.
Needle gauge: use a 27 to 30 gauge needle for drawing from the vial. IV administration requires appropriate IV access.

Kinevac vials are single use Keep the mixed vial at room temperature and discard it after 8 hours; discard a diluted infusion after 1 hour (section 2.2). Keep lyophilized research vials at -20C, protected from light and moisture.
Alternative Routes
Subcutaneous

No human SC bioavailability data available. SC bioavailability likely very low: CCK-8 is rapidly cleaved by plasma peptidases (t½ about 1.3 min IV) and subcutaneous peptidase activity would similarly degrade the peptide before systemic absorption. No dose-equivalency data exists.

All published human dosing data for CCK-8 is intravenous, and the Kinevac (sincalide) label lists IV use only. No human study has tested SC dosing, so an SC dose cannot be assumed to match an IV dose.
Oral

Essentially zero systemic bioavailability via oral route: GI proteases degrade the octapeptide entirely before absorption. This is why the body uses endogenous I-cell CCK secretion rather than circulating CCK from oral intake.

Dietary proteins and fats trigger endogenous CCK release from intestinal I-cells: this is the physiological equivalent of "oral CCK supplementation" and is not replicable by ingesting exogenous CCK-8.
Works With
Avoid
Opioid analgesics (morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone, codeine)

Bidirectional antagonism: opioids inhibit gallbladder contraction peripherally (biliary spasm, elevated sphincter of Oddi tone). CCK-8 also opposes opioid analgesia centrally via CCK2 receptor activation in the spinal cord and brain: reducing opioid analgesic efficacy (PMID 1982023). Interaction is clinically relevant in both directions.
Anticholinergic agents (atropine, glycopyrrolate, scopolamine, diphenhydramine)
Block the downstream parasympathetic pathway through which CCK-8 exerts gallbladder contraction and GI motility effects. Substantially attenuate or abolish efficacy of CCK-8 administration.
Somatostatin
Somatostatin inhibits CCK release from duodenal I-cells and suppresses downstream GI responses, opposing satiety and motility effects of exogenous CCK-8.
Somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide)

Same mechanism as native somatostatin: inhibit CCK secretion and blunt GI motility responses. Listed separately because octreotide is commonly used and not in database as a peptide stacking candidate.
Brand Price
Kinevac (sincalide for injection, Bracco Diagnostics): hospital/nuclear medicine department use only; ~$200–400/diagnostic kit; not available to consumers or research peptide buyers
Generic / Research
Research-grade CCK-8 sulfated, sold only as a lab reagent: ~$100–300/mg. NOT part of the standard research-peptide market. Typically sold in 1-5 mg quantities.

The most serious documented risk with CCK-8 is anaphylaxis. Post-marketing surveillance of sincalide (Kinevac) has recorded anaphylactic shock attributed to sodium metabisulfite preservative in some formulations (KINEVAC FDA label, DailyMed). This is rare but potentially fatal, and epinephrine must be available during any administration. Gallbladder-related complications deserve equal weight. CCK-8 causes forceful gallbladder contraction. In patients with undiagnosed gallstones, this can dislodge stones into the cystic or common bile duct. The result can be biliary colic, cholangitis, or acute pancreatitis. This is a hard contraindication, not a precaution. Abdominal ultrasound before any CCK-8 use is mandatory. At standard diagnostic IV doses, the most common adverse effects are abdominal discomfort and nausea, occurring in over 20 percent of subjects. Higher or bolus doses amplify gastrointestinal symptoms considerably: cramping, vomiting, diarrhea, and a sudden urge to defecate from increased intestinal motility. To reduce them, the Kinevac label offers an infusion in place of the 30 to 60 second IV injection (section 5.3). Cardiovascular effects include bradycardia and transient hypotension via vasovagal activation. Heart rate should stay above 50 bpm and systolic blood pressure above 90 mmHg throughout any infusion. Dizziness, flushing, and diaphoresis have been reported. Neurological side effects are uncommon. Headache occurs occasionally; seizures are documented but very rare. All validated human dosing data is IV only. No human subcutaneous bioavailability data exists. CCK-8 is rapidly cleaved by plasma peptidases, and subcutaneous delivery likely produces negligible systemic levels. The FDA-approved sincalide label specifies IV-only administration. The compound's half-life of about 1.3 minutes means most side effects resolve within minutes of stopping the infusion. That rapid clearance is reassuring for acute tolerability but also means CCK-8 simply does not lend itself to repeated self-administration protocols. In pregnancy, the Kinevac label warns that sincalide may cause preterm labor or spontaneous abortion through its effect on smooth muscle (sections 5.4 and 8.1). Intestinal obstruction is a label contraindication, and active acute pancreatitis is a hard stop too. Stop any infusion immediately for severe abdominal pain, hypotension, bradycardia below 50 bpm, or any sign of allergic reaction. Seek emergency medical care if anaphylaxis is suspected.
Common Issues & Solutions

Nausea and abdominal cramping during administration: the Kinevac label links these to IV injection (section 5.3). To reduce them, it gives an infusion of 0.12 mcg/kg in 100 mL of 0.9% saline over 50 minutes (section 2.1).

Insufficient satiety response: Verify infusion begins 15-30 min before meal (not during or after). Timing relative to meal initiation is critical: the satiety signal must arrive before the cephalic phase terminates.

Effect duration too short: Expected: half-life is about 1.3 min and the direct peptide effect is brief. Downstream neural satiety signaling via the vagus-NTS-hypothalamic axis persists beyond peptide clearance. If longer effect is needed, use continuous infusion rather than bolus.

Gallbladder pain during or after infusion: Stop immediately and assess for stone dislodgement. Biliary colic, cholangitis, or acute pancreatitis are possible sequelae. Ultrasound should rule out cholelithiasis before any CCK-8 administration.

Insufficient biological activity: Confirm the material is the sulfated form (CCK-8S): the sulfated tyrosine at position 7 (Tyr(SO3H)-Met-Gly-Trp-Met-Asp-Phe-NH2) is required for full CCK1 receptor potency. Non-sulfated CCK-8 has ~1000-fold lower CCK1 affinity.

Cholecystokinin (CCK-8): Product Quality high risk

CCK-8 is used IV in research: purity is critical. Unlike SC peptides where mild impurities cause local reactions, IV administration of contaminated peptide risks systemic reactions including anaphylaxis. CCK-8 is a specialty biochemical sold as a lab reagent, not a standard "research peptide" product. Sulfate ester stability, non-sulfated vs. sulfated forms, and lyophilization quality vary significantly across products.
CCK-8 is sold only as a lab reagent for research; pharmaceutical-quality manufacturing matters for IV use. Do not use gray-market peptides for anything given IV.
Before any IV use, a Certificate of Analysis (CoA) should show HPLC purity ≥98% and mass spectrometry confirmation (MW = 1143.25 Da for CCK-8S).
Confirm sulfated form (CCK-8S): product name must specify "sulfated": non-sulfated CCK-8 has ~1000x lower CCK1 receptor potency and will not produce the expected satiety or gallbladder effects.
Check for sulfite preservatives in the lyophilized product: sodium metabisulfite increases anaphylaxis risk; this is the same mechanism as documented anaphylaxis with Kinevac (sincalide).
Store properly at -20°C desiccated in single-use aliquots; the sulfate ester is susceptible to hydrolysis at room temperature and repeated freeze-thaw cycles.

Am J Gastroenterol 1985; PMID 4014106: CCK-8 disappearance half-time 1.30 min after a 2-minute IV infusion in healthy adults (1.70 min in chronic renal failure, 2.45 min in cirrhosis). CCK-8 (cholecystokinin octapeptide, sulfated) is FDA-approved only as a diagnostic agent, under the name sincalide. FDA approved Kinevac (Bracco Diagnostics, NDA 017697) in 1976 and a second sincalide product (NDA 210850) in 2022, both prescription IV drugs. Sincalide is used for gallbladder ejection fraction testing and pancreatic secretion stimulation during imaging studies. Neither approval covers appetite, weight loss or any other therapeutic use. Native CCK-8 is sold only as a lab reagent for research, not for human use. It is not scheduled as a controlled substance and carries no DEA restrictions. It is absent from the standard research-peptide market and has no compounding pharmacy availability. Kinevac is restricted to hospital and nuclear medicine departments. No WADA prohibition exists for CCK specifically, though any peptide used for performance modification may fall under the catch-all prohibition on peptide hormones. This compound has no documented recreational, anabolic, or performance use. This content is for informational and research purposes only. It does not constitute medical advice. Consult a qualified healthcare provider before any investigational use.

faqs.q: Can CCK-8 be used subcutaneously for weight loss?
faqs.a: No published human data supports SC administration. All validated human dosing is IV. The peptide is rapidly degraded by plasma proteases, and SC delivery may produce negligible systemic levels. The diagnostic analog sincalide is IV-only per FDA labeling.

faqs.q: Why is the half-life only about 1.3 minutes?
faqs.a: CCK-8 is rapidly cleaved by circulating peptidases including procollagen C-endopeptidase and other serum proteases. This reflects normal physiology. CCK is a meal-triggered hormone designed for burst signaling, not sustained circulation.

faqs.q: Does CCK-8 cause anxiety or panic?
faqs.a: The closely related fragment CCK-4 (the C-terminal tetrapeptide) is a well-established panicogenic agent in research. CCK-8 has anxiogenic properties at CNS CCK2 receptors but this effect is far weaker than CCK-4. Elevated CCK tone is associated with panic disorder pathophysiology.

faqs.q: Is sincalide the same as CCK-8?
faqs.a: Yes, sincalide is the synthetic C-terminal octapeptide of CCK, identical to CCK-8. Kinevac (sincalide for injection) has been FDA-approved since 1976 for gallbladder function testing.

faqs.q: What happens if someone with gallstones uses CCK-8?
faqs.a: CCK-8 causes forceful gallbladder contraction. In patients with gallstones this can dislodge stones into the cystic duct or common bile duct, causing biliary colic, cholangitis, or acute pancreatitis. This is a hard contraindication. Not a precaution.

summary: Your body already makes CCK-8 every time you eat fat or protein. This sulfated octapeptide fires from duodenal I-cells and tells your brain to stop eating, usually within minutes. Cholecystokinin (CCK-8) is one of the strongest short-term satiety signals in human physiology, and its synthetic twin sincalide (Kinevac) has been FDA-approved since 1976 for gallbladder imaging. The catch: a plasma half-life of about 1.3 minutes makes it nearly useless outside a clinical IV setting. Researchers still study it to understand appetite regulation and gut-brain signaling, but nobody is pinning this one at home.
